summary:
Drasko Profirovic, a Staff Engineer at Pinterest, presents Medic for Apache Spark, an agentic diagnostics tool designed to troubleshoot Spark job failures at scale. The motivation stems from the high volume of support requests in data platform organizations and the difficulty of troubleshooting distributed systems, especially for newcomers. The vision was to ask an agent why a job failed and receive a detailed research document with root-cause evidence and context-grounded remediation suggestions, available on surfaces like Slack and the Airflow UI.

The project began by exposing data resources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect them to LLMs. This was extended into a single ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) agent with one prompt covering problem-solving approach, report structure, and common failure patterns. Early trials revealed significant shortcomings: prompt tuning became unsustainable as one prompt handled everything, response quality was inconsistent, context windows were consumed by large log outputs, and manual end-to-end testing was anecdotal and unreliable.

To address these issues, the team invested in observability via OpenTelemetry traces published to LangFuse, enabling waterfall-diagram analysis of agent steps. They built an end-to-end test harness with record and playback modes: in record mode, real downstream calls are captured as fixtures and checked into version control; in playback mode, the agent runs against fixtures and is graded by offline evaluations such as limiting suggested fixes to three. Log handling was overhauled with an exception classifier pipeline that fingerprints, clusters, and ranks exceptions by relevance and recency, filtering benign exceptions learned from successful jobs. The agent accesses logs through two MCP tools rather than consuming them directly. Metrics handling was improved by a quarantine sub-agent that converts raw time-series data into annotated graph images, guaranteeing fixed token usage regardless of job duration.

The architecture evolved from a single ReAct agent to a multi-agent system built on LangGraph's deep agent library, with each agent having a dedicated prompt and tool subset, plus built-in tools like to-do lists and virtual file systems. The workflow classifies user intent, generates failure hypotheses, researches them in parallel, selects the highest-confidence root cause, and invokes a healer agent for remediations based on runbooks in a vector database. LangGraph's deterministic workflows were tried but proved brittle compared to the ReAct paradigm. Future directions include incorporating user feedback for automatic improvement and expanding to other distributed systems like Flink and Trino.

takeaways: A single ReAct agent with one monolithic prompt proved unsustainable—prompt tuning degraded behavior across areas, response quality was inconsistent, and context windows were overwhelmed by large log outputs.
An end-to-end test harness with record/playback modes and offline evaluations enabled quantified quality measurement and regression detection, replacing anecdotal manual testing.

An exception classifier pipeline—fingerprinting, clustering, and ranking exceptions by relevance and recency—significantly improved signal-to-noise ratio and reduced LLM anchoring on misleading exceptions.
Converting raw time-series metrics into annotated graph images via a sub-agent guaranteed fixed token usage regardless of job duration and kept the parent agent's context window healthy.

Migrating from a single agent to a multi-agent architecture on LangGraph's deep agent library enabled clear separation of concerns, easier prompt maintenance, and simple scope expansion by just adding a new prompt.

The production workflow classifies intent, generates failure hypotheses, researches them in parallel, selects the highest-confidence root cause, and assembles remediation reports from runbook-based suggestions.
LangGraph's deterministic workflows were tested but proved brittle compared to the reasoning-and-acting (ReAct) agent paradigm.
Future work includes using user feedback from prior sessions to automatically improve the agent and expanding the pattern to other distributed systems like Flink and Trino.

sections.title: Introduction & Background
sections.summary: Drasko introduces himself as a Staff Engineer at Pinterest. He discusses the challenges of supporting data platform infrastructure, including the never-ending stream of support questions, the difficulty of troubleshooting distributed systems like Spark, and the ambiguity of prioritizing competing support requests.

sections.title: Vision for Diagnostics Agent
sections.summary: The vision was to ask an agent why a job failed and receive a deep research document with root-cause evidence and context-grounded remediation suggestions. The agent needed to be available on surfaces like Slack and the Airflow UI. Unlike humans, LLMs can scale knowledge on demand.

sections.title: Prototype with MCP and Single ReAct Agent
sections.summary: The project started by exposing data resources via Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect them to LLMs. This was extended into a single ReAct agent with one prompt embodying the problem-solving approach, report structure, and common failure pattern examples. Early beta trials began at this point.

sections.title: Shortcomings of the Single-Agent Approach
sections.summary: Early trials revealed: prompt tuning became unsustainable as one prompt handled everything and changes in one area degraded another; response quality was inconsistent (shallow or too verbose); no controls to keep the agent on track; context window issues from large log tool outputs; and reliance on manual testing from production data that was retentioned away.

sections.title: Observability & End-to-End Test Harness
sections.summary: The team used OpenTelemetry to publish traces to LangFuse for waterfall-diagram analysis. They built an end-to-end test harness with record mode (capturing real downstream calls as fixtures checked into code) and playback mode (running agent against fixtures, graded by offline evals such as limiting suggested fixes to three). This enabled quantified quality measurement and regression detection.

sections.title: Log Handling & Exception Classifier Pipeline
sections.summary: Logs are noisy with many benign exceptions. Regex filtering did not scale. The team built an exception classifier pipeline that learns which exceptions appear in successful jobs (treated as red herrings), fingerprints and clusters exceptions, and ranks them by content relevance and recency to job termination. The agent accesses logs via two MCP tools: get top K truncated exceptions or get full details for a specific exception. This improved signal-to-noise ratio and reduced LLM anchoring on misleading exceptions.

sections.title: Metrics Handling via Graph Images
sections.summary: Raw time-series metrics are not context-window friendly. A quarantine sub-agent converts raw data into graphs collaged into a final image resembling a Grafana dashboard with annotations like min/max values. The image is attached to the LLM conversation, guaranteeing fixed token usage regardless of job duration. Useful signals include executors dropping to zero, long plateaus, and resource behavior inconsistent with healthy progress. The sub-agent returns summaries to the parent agent, keeping the context window healthy.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Architecture on LangGraph
sections.summary: The system evolved from a single ReAct agent to a multi-agent architecture built on LangGraph's deep agent library. Each agent has a dedicated prompt and subset of MCP tools, with built-in tools like to-do lists and virtual file systems. This refactor decomposed the monolithic prompt into specialized roles, enabled focused testing, and made scope expansion as simple as adding a new prompt—extending Medic to Spark SQL optimization.

sections.title: Production Workflow & Scope Expansion
sections.summary: The workflow classifies user intent (simple answer vs. deep diagnostic). For diagnostics, a triage agent determines job lifecycle state and generates failure hypotheses. Each hypothesis is researched in parallel, returning a score and root cause. The supervisor selects the highest-confidence root cause and invokes a healer agent for remediations based on runbooks in a vector database. The supervisor assembles the final report.

sections.title: Results & Future Directions
sections.summary: The multi-agent architecture proved very effective, offering the greatest control over system behavior. Log handling improvements led to substantial reduction in inaccurate root causes. LangGraph's deterministic workflows were tried but proved brittle vs. ReAct. Future work includes incorporating user feedback from prior sessions for automatic improvement and expanding to other distributed systems like Flink and Trino.
